## 1. Verse-by-verse: the traditional reading

**v. 1**
- "At that time" probably doesn't mean the day the wall was dedicated. Benson places it after Nehemiah came back from Persia. The Pulpit Commentary reads it as "about that time." The Layman's Bible Commentary calls it a general phrase for an unspecified time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/13-1.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nehemiah-13.html
- The law being read is Deuteronomy 23:3–4. Guzik says Ammonites and Moabites could still belong to Israel if they turned to Israel's God, but they had to choose it, leaving their own gods behind. EW
- Gill takes "come into the congregation" to mean being allowed to marry Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-13.html
- Utley admits the rule "sounds so racist to us." He gives two replies: the returning community had to stay free of pagan culture, and Ruth the Moabite is an ancestor of David and of the Messiah. He also notes this is the only Old Testament verse that joins *qahal* ("assembly") with "God," and that the Greek Old Testament translates *qahal* with *ecclesia*, the word the early church used for itself. Utley

**v. 2**
- Guzik sees this as Genesis 12:3 being fulfilled ("I will curse him who curses you"). The background is Numbers 22–24, and he says it shows God can turn any curse into a blessing. EW
- Utley notes that Ammon and Moab were relatives of Israel (Genesis 19). He calls the Balaam story "strange and bizarre," and treats "turned the curse into a blessing" as a major theme across Scripture, seen in Abraham, Joseph and Moses. Utley

**v. 3**
- Guzik praises the people for obeying at once, with no excuses like "things are different now." He takes the "mixed multitude" to mean people who joined themselves to Israel without really taking up the covenant. He compares them to well-meaning churchgoers who haven't received salvation in Jesus. EW
- Utley points out that the same Hebrew word describes the believing Egyptians who left Egypt with Israel in Exodus 12:38. He concludes the word is used in a religious sense, not a racial one. Utley

**v. 4**
- Benson says Eliashib was "allied" to Tobiah, an enemy of God's people. He links this to the marriage of Eliashib's grandson to Sanballat's daughter (v. 28) and calls it a great blot on Eliashib's character. Benson
- The Hebrew word means "near," so it could mean a neighbour or a relative. Utley says Eliashib later becomes high priest. Utley
- The Pulpit Commentary says Eliashib was tied to Tobiah by marriage. Pulpit
- The Bridgeway Bible Commentary holds the high priest mainly to blame for the decline. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/13-28.html

**v. 5**
- The storerooms held the Levites' tithes and the supplies for worship. The people tithed to the Levites, and the Levites tithed to the priests. Utley
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The Hebrew could mean either Eliashib or Tobiah did this. Eliashib probably let Tobiah furnish rooms in the temple, where the law didn't allow him. One older writer (Tirinus) says Tobiah rented the rooms and managed the priests' income. Haydock

**v. 6**
- Utley dates Nehemiah's time as governor to 445–433 BC. He explains that Persian kings, including Cyrus and Darius, are also called "king of Babylon." Utley
- Guzik thinks Nehemiah was away for 10 to 12 years. He says the real test of a revival is where people stand years later. EW

**v. 7**
- Utley says it's unclear which court is meant, but no one except Levites was allowed in that area. Utley

**v. 8**
- Guzik compares this to Jesus cleansing the temple: both knew love isn't the same as being "nice." He adds that Tobiah, an Ammonite, was exactly the kind of person excluded in v. 1–3. EW
- Utley says Nehemiah "was not a gentle man as was Ezra." His anger was both personal and religious. Utley

**v. 9**
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The rooms needed cleansing because a pagan had profaned them. The "offerings" (Hebrew *mincha*) were flour, fruit and drink offerings that Eliashib had moved out to make space for Tobiah. Haydock

**v. 10**
- The Levites had a small amount of land near their towns to add to what the people gave them, and that's where they went (Numbers 35; Joshua 21). Utley
- Guzik says failing to give was a way of turning one's back on God. EW
- The Pulpit Commentary says the Levites' absence took dignity away from temple worship. Pulpit

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry says Nehemiah blamed the rulers. He draws the lesson that Christian magistrates should use their power to make ministers and people do their duty. MH
- The Hebrew verb ("rebuked") is a legal word for a dispute or court case, which shows how serious this was. The same verb appears in v. 17 and v. 25. Utley

**v. 12–13**
- Nehemiah chose trustworthy treasurers from different groups (a priest, a scribe, a Levite). The Hebrew word for "trustworthy" is the root of "amen." Utley

**v. 14**
- Benson says Nehemiah isn't boasting or making God his debtor. He is humbly appealing to God about the honesty of his motives. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/13-14.htm
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary points out that Nehemiah prays "Remember me," not "Reward me." Same page.
- The Cambridge Bible explains "do not blot out" as a picture of wiping writing off a leather scroll (compare Exodus 32:32–33). Same page.
- The Pulpit Commentary prefers "observances" to "services," meaning the rites and customs of worship. Same page.
- Nehemiah uses the Hebrew word *hesed* (loving devotion) for his own deeds here. In v. 22 he uses it for God's faithfulness. Utley

**v. 15–16**
- Matthew Henry notes that harvest work on the Sabbath was specifically forbidden (Exodus 34:21). He says religion "is never in the throne while sabbaths are trodden under foot." MH
- Utley says Jews themselves were now trading on the Sabbath, not just foreigners. He links this to Exodus 31:14 and Jeremiah 17:19–27. Utley
- Pett connects Nehemiah's action to Jeremiah 17, which promised blessing on Jerusalem if the Sabbath was kept. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-13.html
- Guzik sees the root problem as priorities: making and spending money had come before honouring God. EW

**v. 17–18**
- Matthew Henry says the nobles were guilty because they allowed it and because their own example was bad. MH
- Guzik says open sin left uncorrected among God's people invites God's correction. EW
- Utley argues that the Mosaic covenant depended on human obedience, which was doomed by the Fall (Genesis 3). That points ahead to a new covenant based on what the Messiah does. Utley

**v. 19**
- The Pulpit Commentary says Nehemiah shut the gates early, as shadows lengthened, because he thought working right up to the last minute dishonoured the Sabbath. Pulpit
- Matthew Henry says the gates stayed shut from the evening before to the morning after, so Sabbath time couldn't be eaten into. MH
- **Catholic (Haydock):** The Sabbath began on Friday night, and that's when the gates were shut. Haydock

**v. 20–21**
- Merchants camping outside the walls would tempt people to go out and buy, and simply having them there caused trouble. Utley
- Guzik: "lay hands on you" meant rough correction, not the gentle laying on of hands for prayer. EW

**v. 22**
- Nehemiah treated the whole city as holy, which is why Levites guarded the gates. Utley also notes a paradox: Nehemiah asks God to remember his deeds, but bases the request on God's *hesed*. Utley
- The Pulpit Commentary and Matthew Henry both think the reform lasted. By Jesus' day, Jews were even "over-scrupulous" about the Sabbath. Pulpit ; MH

**v. 23**
- Gill: Ashdod wasn't one of the seven nations Israel was forbidden to marry, but marriage there was still "unfit." He says Ashdod was a market town where Jews could get drawn into these marriages. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-13.html
- Utley calls intermarriage a problem that keeps coming back, which neither Ezra nor Nehemiah solved. Utley

**v. 24**
- Utley says the Hebrew idiom is unclear. The point is that pagan mothers were raising the children, so the children couldn't understand God's word in Hebrew. Utley
- Matthew Henry's Concise Commentary applies this to raising children: they shouldn't learn "the language of Ashdod," meaning ungodly talk. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/13-25.htm

**v. 25**
- Ellicott: by cursing them, Nehemiah was repeating the penalty the people had sworn to themselves in the covenant (10:29–30). Only some were singled out for punishment. Ezra, by contrast, pulled out his own hair (Ezra 9:3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/13-25.htm
- Benson softens the verse. "Cursed" means he excluded them from the community. "Smote" means officers beat them under Deuteronomy 25:2. "Plucked off their hair" means they were shaved to shame them. Same page.
- Clarke reads it similarly: a legal hearing, a whipping, and a shaved head as disgrace. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/nehemiah/13-25.html
- Constable says pulling out the beard was a punishment and a public disgrace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/13-25.html
- A Bible Hub article calls the passage descriptive, not prescriptive. It says the principle carries over to today, but the physical punishment does not. https://biblehub.com/q/Nehemiah_13_25_s_role_in_the_book.htm
- Guzik thinks Nehemiah saw this as the most dangerous of the people's sins. EW

**v. 26–27**
- Guzik: if someone as wise and blessed as Solomon fell this way, nobody should think they are safe from it. EW

**v. 28**
- Josephus names the expelled priest Manasseh. He says Sanballat then built him a rival temple on Mount Gerizim, which started the Samaritan rivalry. MH, Benson and Poole all repeat this. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/13-28.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/13-28.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the man probably refused to give up his wife and fled to Samaria. Pulpit
- Keil & Delitzsch call the idea of two different Sanballats "very improbable." They blame Josephus's notoriously unreliable dating. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/nehemiah/13-28.htm
- The Cambridge Bible calls Rashi's explanation, that Nehemiah feared the man would spy on the city, "strangely inadequate." Same page.
- Constable says marriages between leading families were often political alliances. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/nehemiah/13-24.html
- **Catholic (Haydock):** If Josephus's dating were right, Sanballat would have been 150 years old. Haydock notes that some therefore think there were two Sanballats. Haydock

**v. 29**
- Matthew Henry gives two readings of "Remember them." Either it's a prayer for God to bring them to their senses, or a prayer for God to hold the sin against them, which would make it a prophecy. MH
- Pett says "them" must mean the high priest's family. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/nehemiah-13.html

**v. 30–31**
- Guzik notes that the people broke the same three promises they made in chapter 10: their marriages, the Sabbath, and support for the temple. His conclusion is that vows can't stop sin; only God's grace can (Romans 8:3). EW
- Matthew Henry: Nehemiah "takes him for his paymaster," meaning he looks to God for his reward. MH

## 2. Where Christian teachers differ

I didn't find enough to set out separate Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed, Lutheran or Anglican positions verse by verse. The one clear split I found is over **v. 15–22 and how the Sabbath applies to Christians**:
- **Keeping the Fourth Commandment:** Matthew Henry treats the passage as upholding the Fourth Commandment and says rulers should use their power to protect the day. MH. The Pulpit Commentary applies it to the Lord's Day and urges Sunday worship. Pulpit
- **A middle view:** Alexander MacLaren says the Lord's Day "is not the Jewish Sabbath." He thinks religious observance shouldn't be enforced by law and warns against overly rigid keeping. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/nehemiah/sabbath-observance.cfm. A summary of his view adds that Nehemiah's example is no pattern for Christians "without many limitations." https://biblehub.com/topical/naves/s/sabbath--observance_of_by_nehemiah.htm
- **Not under the Sabbath law:** Guzik says Christians aren't under the Sabbath law (Colossians 2:16–17), but must still put God before money. EW. The bible.org series agrees: "we are not under the strict Sabbath laws of Israel." https://bible.org/seriespage/lesson-13-problem-permissiveness-nehemiah-131-31

A smaller point on **v. 14, 22 and 31 ("Remember me")**: a sermon on Bible Hub insists Nehemiah "cannot make them a plea for merit before God" and relies on free grace. https://biblehub.com/sermons/nehemiah/13-25.htm. Benson says the same (see v. 14).

**On v. 23–27, a Reformed devotional on the parallel passage in Ezra 9:** Ligonier says the sin wasn't marrying someone of another race. It was marrying pagans who hadn't repented, which is why Ruth was accepted once she converted. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/problem-of-intermarriage

## 3. Other views

**Modern scholarship**
- **v. 23–27:** Bible Odyssey says the text reflects a growing sense of ethnic identity among those who came back from exile. It notes that many anthropologists see ethnicity as something a community constructs, and that many other parts of the Hebrew Bible don't object to intermarriage the way Ezra and Nehemiah do. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/intermarriage-in-ezra-nehemiah/
- A second Bible Odyssey article links this fear of mixed marriage to the foreign "Lady Foolishness" figure in Proverbs. https://bibleodyssey.org/people/related-articles/immigrants-and-foreigners-in-the-bible
- **v. 23:** The Layman's Bible Commentary concludes Ezra's earlier reform wasn't as successful as Ezra's account suggests. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nehemiah-13.html
- **v. 13:** Some scholars use this verse to argue Ezra came after Nehemiah. Utley says we know too little to decide. Utley
- **Archaeology (v. 15, v. 28):** Bible Hub mentions the Elephantine papyri (about 407 BC), which name a high priest Johanan and a "Sanballat governor of Samaria," and Yavneh-Yam inscriptions about the Sabbath. https://biblehub.com/study/chapters/nehemiah/13.htm ; https://biblehub.com/nehemiah/13.htm

**Catholic:** Haydock's notes are given under v. 5, 9, 19 and 28.
